title: Symphony No. 1 in B-flat major, “Spring”
hook: Sketched in four days in a Leipzig January, a symphony that wakes up with a trumpet call.

painting.title: Bridal Procession in a Spring Landscape
painting.collection: Galerie Neue Meister, Staatliche Kunstsammlungen Dresden
painting.pairingNote: A wedding party walks through a wood in spring, painted in Dresden by the artist who drew the title page of Schumann’s Album for the Young; the symphony was written in the first winter of Schumann’s marriage.

facts: Until 1840 Schumann wrote almost only for the piano, and then, in the year of his marriage to Clara Wieck, mostly songs. Clara wanted more. She wrote in her diary that his imagination could not find enough room on the piano and that her dearest wish was for him to compose for orchestra.

He sketched this symphony in four days, 23 to 26 January 1841, and finished the scoring by 20 February. Mendelssohn conducted the first performance in Leipzig on 31 March 1841, with the Gewandhaus Orchestra. It was warmly received.

The idea of spring came from a poem by Adolf Böttger that ends with the words “in the valley, spring blooms forth”. Schumann first gave the movements titles: “The Beginning of Spring”, “Evening”, “Merry Playmates” and “Spring in Full Bloom”. He removed them before publication.

Later he wrote to a conductor that the first trumpet call should sound “as if it came from on high, like a summons to awakening”, and that the introduction might suggest the world turning green. He added that these images came to him only after the music was finished.
bigPicture.inOneLine: winter breaking into spring (I), an evening song (II), a sturdy dance with two contrasting episodes (III), spring in full bloom (IV).

movements.heading: Andante un poco maestoso – Allegro molto vivace
movements.tempo: Andante un poco maestoso – Allegro molto vivace
movements.summary: Trumpets and horns call out a short fanfare, and the whole orchestra answers. A slow, mysterious introduction follows, then the music speeds up, and the fanfare’s rhythm becomes the quick main theme. It is a [[sonata-form|sonata form]] movement full of energy, with a new, singing tune saved for the end.

mainIdeas.name: The fanfare
mainIdeas.description: a short, bold call in trumpets and horns, in the rhythm of the poem’s last line.

mainIdeas.name: The Allegro theme
mainIdeas.description: the same rhythm, now fast and bouncing, for the whole orchestra.

mainIdeas.name: Theme 2
mainIdeas.description: a gentle, swaying tune in the woodwind.

stops.hear: Trumpets and horns play a bold call; the whole orchestra answers loudly
Quiet and hushed; soft woodwind figures and murmuring strings
stops.happening: The slow introduction: the world turning green

stops.hear: The music gathers speed and grows louder
stops.happening: The introduction runs into the Allegro

stops.hear: Fast and bright: the fanfare’s rhythm, now bouncing along
A gentler, swaying tune in clarinets and bassoons
The fast, bouncing theme again from the start
The main rhythm is broken up and passed around, through changing keys
The opening fanfare returns, loud and broad, in the whole orchestra
A new, flowing tune in the strings
stops.happening: The [[coda|coda]] brings a melody not heard before

stops.label: Last 20 seconds
stops.hear: A quick, bright ending
stops.happening: The movement ends in B-flat major

notice: Compare the fanfare at the start with the fast theme at ≈ 1:45. They share the same rhythm, first slow and solemn, then quick and bouncing.
Listen for the new tune at ≈ 9:30. Schumann keeps one fresh idea back until the very end of the movement.

notes.title: In this recording
notes.body: Gardiner’s orchestra plays on period instruments, the kind of orchestra Schumann wrote for in 1841.

movements.heading: Larghetto
movements.summary: The “Evening” movement: a long, warm song passed from the violins to the cellos and then to the woodwind. At the very end the trombones enter softly with a quiet, falling phrase. It leads straight into the [[scherzo|scherzo]].

mainIdeas.name: The song
mainIdeas.description: a long, singing melody, first in the violins, then in the cellos.

mainIdeas.name: The trombone phrase
mainIdeas.description: soft and solemn, a hint of the scherzo to come.

stops.hear: The violins sing a long, tender melody
The cellos take over the melody, the violins weave around it
stops.happening: The theme in a deeper voice

stops.hear: Oboe and horn share the song; the harmony wanders
The melody returns in the violins, richer than before
The trombones play softly, a slow, falling phrase like a hymn

stops.label: Last 20 seconds
stops.hear: The music stops on an open chord, waiting
stops.happening: It leads straight into the scherzo without a break

notice: Listen for the trombones at the end. Their few soft notes become the start of the next movement’s theme.

movements.heading: Scherzo: Molto vivace
movements.summary: A strong, stamping dance in D minor, with two contrasting [[trio|trio]] sections. The first trio is quick and light, in two beats instead of three; the second is a stream of running notes. The scherzo returns after each, and the movement ends quietly with a memory of the first trio.

mainIdeas.name: The scherzo
mainIdeas.description: a sturdy, accented tune in three beats, grown from the trombones’ phrase.

mainIdeas.name: Trio 1
mainIdeas.description: quick, light chords tossed between wind and strings, in two beats.

mainIdeas.name: Trio 2
mainIdeas.description: a busy stream of running notes.

stops.hear: A strong, stamping dance tune in a minor key
Lighter and quicker, in two beats: short chords bounce between wind and strings
The stamping dance returns
A rush of running notes passed around the orchestra
The dance tune once more
The light chords of the first trio come back, slower and softer, and fade away

notice: Count the beats. The scherzo moves in three, the first trio in two; you can feel the change in your body.

movements.heading: Allegro animato e grazioso
movements.summary: “Spring in full bloom”. After a rising scale for the whole orchestra, a light, dancing theme takes over. Before the themes return, the music stops: the horns play a soft call, and a solo flute answers with a free, birdlike run. Schumann asked for the movement not to be taken too frivolously.

mainIdeas.name: The opening
mainIdeas.description: a broad scale rising through the orchestra, like a door flung open.

mainIdeas.name: The horn call and the flute’s answer
mainIdeas.description: a pause in the open air.

stops.hear: A rising scale for the whole orchestra, then a light, dancing theme
A second, playful theme with short, crisp notes
The rising scale and dancing theme again
The themes are worked over, louder and more insistent
Everything stops; the horns call softly, and a solo flute answers with a free, rising run
The dancing theme comes back
Faster and louder, a joyful rush to the end

notice: Listen for the horns and flute at ≈ 5:00. The orchestra falls silent and two solo voices take over, like a call and an echo in a wood.

threads.title: Spring in winter
threads.body: The symphony was written in January, in a few days, in the first winter of Schumann’s marriage. It looks forward to spring rather than describing it.

threads.title: The trumpet call
threads.body: The opening rhythm returns as the Allegro theme and again at the recapitulation; the trombones’ phrase at the end of the Larghetto becomes the scherzo’s tune. The movements are linked by shared ideas.

threads.title: A piano composer’s orchestra
threads.body: It was Schumann’s first finished symphony. The finale even borrows a theme from the last piece of his piano cycle *Kreisleriana* (1838).

threads.title: Colour
threads.body: Schumann asked for three timpani, which was rare at the time, and added a triangle to the orchestra.
